chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Sayf al-Tammār, who said:

I said to Abu Baseer, 'I would like you to ask Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who exchanged two baskets containing cooked unripened dates for one basket containing split dates.' He said, 'So Abu Baseer asked him about that, so he (peace be upon him) said: 'This is disliked.' Abu Baseer said, 'And why is it disliked?' He said, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) disliked that one wasq of the dates of Medina be exchanged for two wasqs of the dates of Khyber, because the dates of Medina were the inferior of the two, and it never happened that Ali (peace be upon him) disliked the permissible.'

key_terms.مَكْرُوهٌ: disliked (recommended to avoid but not forbidden)

ai.seo_question: Why is exchanging inferior dates for superior dates in larger quantity considered disliked in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the distinction between *karāhah* (dislike) and *ḥarām* (forbidden) in commercial transactions, using Imam Ali’s (AS) practice of avoiding the exchange of superior Medinan dates for inferior Khaybar dates despite the quantity difference. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on *iḥsān* (excellence) and fairness in trade, where the higher-quality item is preserved for its intrinsic value rather than merely compensating for quantity. The narration serves as a practical legal precedent for evaluating commodity quality in Islamic jurisprudence.
